summary: This unit teaches you to provide workplace mentoring: to understand what mentoring is and how it differs from coaching, supervision and counselling; to prepare, agree a mentoring agreement and keep confidentiality and boundaries; to set SMART goals with the GROW model; to use listening, questioning and feedback; to deal with problems and end the relationship well; and to help run and evaluate a mentoring scheme.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. **Workplace mentoring** is a longer-term relationship in which an experienced person (the **mentor**) guides the growth of a less experienced person (the **mentee**). At Level 5 you are expected to act as a mentor, to prepare other mentors, and to help design and run a scheme in a hotel, school, ministry, agency or business.

In Jamaica, mentoring is used to help new supervisors settle in, to support newly qualified teachers, to prepare officers for promotion, to pass skills on before experienced staff retire, and to keep good people from leaving. It works only when the mentee trusts the mentor, so most of this unit is about trust, listening and boundaries.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Explain what mentoring is
Define mentoring, compare it with coaching, line management and counselling, and name its benefits and types.
Prepare to mentor and match well
Know the qualities of a mentor, match people on needs and goals, and prepare before the first meeting.
Start the relationship properly
Build rapport, agree a mentoring agreement and explain confidentiality and its limits.
Set goals and plan learning
Help the mentee find learning needs and turn vague wishes into SMART goals, using a model such as GROW.
Use mentoring skills
Listen actively, ask open questions, give useful feedback, share experience wisely and encourage reflection.
Keep boundaries and handle problems
Stay within the mentor's role, deal with dependency, missed meetings, differences and serious concerns.
Review and end the relationship
Review progress, keep brief notes, close the relationship well and keep learning as a mentor.
Help run and evaluate a scheme
Plan purpose, matching, training and measures such as retention, and show the results.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** of scenario questions, including short sums on hours and percentages.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as GROW, rapport, boundaries) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical tasks** done in a group: role-play a first mentoring meeting and write a mentoring agreement and SMART goals; and design a one-year mentoring scheme and present it to management.

blocks.note: Learn the key terms in the Revision section. Short answers ask for exact words such as mentee, GROW, reverse mentoring and reflection.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Mentoring is a **developmental relationship**. The mentor shares experience, asks questions, gives feedback and opens doors, but the mentee does the learning and makes the decisions. It is usually voluntary, confidential and agreed for a period (for example 6 to 12 months). The mentor is not the mentee's boss and does not do the mentee's job.

head: Role
Focus
Time
Who decides
rows: Mentoring
Broad growth: career, confidence, understanding the organisation
Longer term, often 6 to 12 months or more
The mentee decides; the mentor guides
Coaching
Specific skills or goals, such as running meetings or using a system
Shorter, tied to a goal
Coach and coachee agree the goal and practice
Line management (supervision)
Day-to-day work, standards, appraisal
Continuous
The manager sets work and decisions about the job
Training
Teaching a skill or topic to a group or individual
A course or session
Trainer sets content
Counselling
Personal, emotional or health problems
As needed, by trained professionals
The client, with a qualified counsellor

blocks.p: Many organisations **avoid making a person's line manager their mentor**. The line manager appraises the mentee, so the mentee may not speak openly about doubts or mistakes. A mentor from outside the line works better.

head: Type
Description
Example
rows: Formal
Set up by the organisation, with matching, agreement and review
A scheme for newly appointed officers
Informal
Grows naturally between two people
A senior teacher who guides a new colleague
One-to-one
One mentor and one mentee (the usual form)
A manager and a new supervisor
Group
One mentor with a small group
A head of department with several new teachers
Peer mentoring
Between colleagues of similar level
Two new supervisors who share what they learn
Reverse mentoring
A junior person guides a senior one, often on new skills
A young officer helps a director use new digital tools
E-mentoring
Mostly by email, messages and video calls, often across distance
A manager in Kingston supports officers in distant offices

head: Who
Benefits
rows: Mentee
Faster settling in, confidence, clearer goals, new contacts, a safe place to think
Mentor
Better listening and leadership skills, fresh views on the work, satisfaction in developing others (no pay, promotion or authority over the mentee comes with it)
Organisation
Faster induction, better retention of staff, stronger skills passed on, a learning culture

blocks.note: A mentor's reward is the learning and satisfaction of helping someone grow. A mentor never gets an extra payment from the mentee or a guaranteed promotion for mentoring.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In the public sector and large firms, the human resources department or the scheme coordinator usually sets up mentoring schemes and runs the matching. Ask who the scheme lead is and follow the organisation's policy.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: The mentor: qualities, matching and preparation

ul: **Trustworthy**: keeps confidences and keeps promises.
**A good listener**: gives full attention and does not interrupt.
**Willing to give time**: turns up, on time, prepared.
**Experienced and respected**, but seniority alone does not make a good mentor.
**Open and honest**: gives straight, kind feedback.
**Positive and patient**: believes the mentee can grow and lets them find their own answers.
**Self-aware**: knows their own limits and keeps learning.

blocks.p: A mentor does **not** have to be the most senior person available, have the same background as the mentee or solve every problem. In fact, a mentor who solves every problem stops the mentee learning.

Good matching raises the chance that the relationship works. Match on **the mentee's needs and goals**, **the mentor's skills and experience**, and **both people's views** (a short form or meeting). Check for conflicts of interest, such as the mentor being in the mentee's line of reporting. Do not match simply by who has free time, by seniority, or by the choice of senior staff.

head: Poor matching
Better matching
rows: By free periods or time available
By the mentee's goals and the mentor's relevant skills
Senior staff choose their favourites
Both people's preferences are asked and respected
The mentee's line manager is the mentor
A mentor from outside the line of reporting
No chance to change if it does not work
A review and a no-fault way to change after the first few meetings

flow: Learn about the mentee's role and the aims of the scheme
Read only what you are meant to read, not private files such as medical or pay records
Think about what you can offer, and what you cannot
Choose a private, quiet place and about an hour
Plan how to open: introductions, listening, agreement

blocks.note: Do not ask the mentee's colleagues for their opinions of the mentee before you meet, and do not write the goals for the mentee. Goals belong to the mentee.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Starting the relationship: first meeting, agreement, confidentiality

blocks.p: The main aim of the first meeting is to **build rapport** (a feeling of trust and understanding that lets people talk openly) and to **agree how the relationship will work**. Do not try to solve the mentee's most urgent problem in full, to assess the mentee's performance for appraisal, or to tell your whole career history.

flow: Welcome the mentee, relax them and explain how you will use the time
Invite the mentee to talk about herself, her work and her hopes; listen with open questions
Explain what mentoring is and is not, including your limits
Discuss goals and expectations on both sides
Agree how often to meet, how to contact each other and the length of the relationship
Agree confidentiality and its limits
Draft the mentoring agreement and a first goal; set the next meeting

blocks.p: A **mentoring agreement** (or mentoring contract) is a short written understanding, agreed and signed by both people. It protects both. It should cover:

ul: **Goals** the mentee wants to work on
**How often** to meet, for how long, where, and how to contact each other
**Confidentiality** and its limits
**Roles and boundaries**: what the mentor will and will not do
**How progress will be reviewed**, and when
**How the relationship will end**, including a no-fault way out

blocks.p: It does **not** include salaries, promises of promotion, or lists of past mistakes.

Mentoring works only when the mentee can speak openly about doubts, mistakes and ambitions without fear that it will reach her manager or colleagues. So what is said in mentoring is private. But confidentiality has **limits** that must be explained **at the start**, so the mentee knows what stays private and when it might not.

head: Stays private
May have to be shared (explain in advance)
rows: Doubts, mistakes, career ideas, feelings about the work, plans to look at other jobs
A serious risk of harm to the mentee or someone else, abuse, a crime, a serious breach of safety or law, as the agreement and the organisation's policy set out

ul: Share only **what is needed**, only with **the person who can help**, and tell the mentee first where you can.
The mentor does not report on the mentee to the mentee's manager, give the manager an update on her weaknesses, or use the mentee's story in training without permission.
If the mentee's manager asks how she is doing, the mentor says that the sessions are confidential and suggests the manager speaks to the mentee.
Keep notes brief and secure; do not discuss mentoring in public places or on shared devices.

blocks.note: If a mentee tells you she has felt hopeless for weeks or is thinking of harming herself, do not promise secrecy and do not leave it to next month. Take it seriously, stay with her and get urgent help through the proper route in your agreement, such as the employee assistance programme, a doctor or emergency services.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Goals, learning needs and the GROW model

blocks.p: Help the mentee discover what she needs to learn. Do not decide for her from your own first job, rely only on her manager's appraisal ratings, or hand her a list of courses. Use **questions, self-assessment and feedback** to explore her strengths and gaps, and her goals for the next year.

ul: Ask: 'What are you most proud of in the last six months? What was hardest?'
Use a simple self-rating of skills (1 to 5) and talk about the gaps.
With her agreement, use feedback from others and her appraisal as one source among several.

blocks.p: A goal such as 'get better at my job' or 'become a better manager' is too vague to act on. Help the mentee make it **SMART**: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

head: Vague goal
SMART version
rows: Improve my communication skills
Lead two team briefings a month and ask for feedback from the team by 30 March
Become more confident
Present the monthly sales figures to the department at the next three meetings, and note one thing to improve after each
Move into management one day
By December, complete a supervisory course and shadow a manager for two days a month, then discuss in the mentoring sessions
Learn the finance system
Complete the basic training and process 20 invoices a week unaided by the end of the quarter

blocks.p: Limit goals to **two or three** at a time. The mentee chooses them; the mentor helps to shape them.
**GROW** is a four-step structure for a mentoring conversation. It keeps the conversation on the mentee's thinking.

head: Letter
Step
Typical questions
rows: G
Goal
What do you want to achieve? What would success look like? By when?
R
Reality
Where are you now? What have you tried? What is getting in the way?
O
Options
What could you do? What else? What are the pros and cons of each?
W
Way forward (will)
What will you do first? By when? What might stop you? How will we know?

blocks.p: Other models you may meet: **SWOT** (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats) can help a mentee think about her position; **PESTLE** is a tool for analysing an organisation's wider environment, not a mentoring conversation model.

head: Stage (one common model)
What happens
rows: Initiation (starting)
The two people meet, build rapport and agree how to work
Cultivation (building)
The most active stage: goals pursued, skills built, trust deepens
Separation
The mentee becomes more independent; the formal relationship winds down
Redefinition
The relationship ends or becomes a more informal, peer-like contact

blocks.note: Set a review date at the first meeting. Three months in, the pair should review progress on the goals and how the relationship is working, and adjust.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Give your **full attention**: put the phone away, face the mentee, do not plan your next point while she speaks.
Show you are listening with eye contact, a nod and short words of encouragement.
**Summarise** in your own words and check you have it right: 'So the main worry is the workload and the new reports. Is that right?'
Do not finish her sentences or interrupt.
Notice feelings and body language; ask about them gently.

head: Closed question
Open question
rows: Did you finish the report on time?
What got in the way of finishing the report?
Was the meeting a success?
What went well in the meeting, and what would you change?
Do you agree you should have asked first?
What options did you see before you decided?

blocks.p: Open questions help the mentee think for herself. When a mentee asks, 'What should I do about my difficult supervisor?', the best first response is not to say exactly what you would do. Ask what has happened and what options she can see.
Feedback is useful when it is **specific, balanced, about behaviour, kind and soon after the event**, and when it ends with something the mentee can do.

head: Poor feedback
Good feedback
rows: 'That was fine, well done.'
'Your opening got everyone's attention. When you give the figures, slow down so the client can follow.'
'You were nervous; everyone could see.'
'Your hands were shaking at first, but you settled quickly after the first slide.'
'You should do it the way I did when I had your job.'
'What would you try differently next time? Here is one option I have seen work.'

blocks.p: A story from your own career is useful when it **helps the mentee see options**, not when it tells her what to do or shows how successful you are. Offer it after she has explored her own ideas, and let her take what is useful: 'I once faced something similar. Would it help if I shared what I tried?'

**Reflection** means thinking back over an experience to learn from it and plan what to do next. After a new task, ask: What happened? What went well? What would you do differently? What will you try next? Reflection helps the mentee learn from experience; it is not used to find mistakes to report or to make her feel guilty.

ul: Keep promises and keep to times.
Be honest, including about what you do not know.
Respect confidentiality always.
Remember that mentees learn as much from **what you do** as from what you say. Your own behaviour at work is part of the mentoring, though the mentee should not copy everything you do.

blocks.note: A good mentoring meeting is mostly the mentee talking. If you are talking for more than a third of the time, ask yourself whether you are listening enough.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Boundaries, problems, diversity and ending the relationship

blocks.p: **Boundaries** are the limits a mentor keeps so that the relationship stays safe and useful.

head: The mentor is not ...
So the mentor ...
rows: The mentee's manager
Does not give daily instructions or report on performance
A counsellor or therapist
Listens with care, then refers serious personal, family or health problems to the employee assistance programme or other trained help
An advocate who fixes outcomes
Does not influence a selection or promotion decision for the mentee; helps her prepare instead
A friend who shares everything
Keeps the relationship professional and respects privacy
Responsible for the mentee's choices
Helps her explore options; she decides

head: Problem
What the mentor should do
rows: The mentee asks the mentor to make sure she is shortlisted
Explain that you cannot influence the selection, and offer to help her prepare (CV, practice interview)
The mentee depends on you for even small decisions
Encourage her to think through options first, ask what she would do, and build her confidence step by step; do not keep answering every question or decide for her
Serious personal problems at every meeting
Listen with care and refer to the employee assistance programme or other help; do not become her counsellor
The mentee keeps cancelling at short notice
Talk openly about what is getting in the way before deciding anything; do not report her or end the relationship without discussion
The mentee tells you in confidence she plans to leave for another employer
Respect the confidence and help her think through the choice; do not tell her manager
Comments become personal or unwelcome
Stop at once: the relationship must be safe and free of harassment; follow the organisation's policy and the law on harassment
A serious risk of harm is disclosed
Follow the limits of confidentiality in the agreement and get help urgently

blocks.p: Differences in age, gender, background, parish or culture can enrich mentoring or cause misunderstanding. An older mentor may assume that the paths of the past still apply; a younger mentee may see the mentor's advice as out of date. **Stay open, ask about the mentee's views, avoid assumptions** and do not expect her to adopt your ways of working and thinking. Do not avoid talk about background, and do not demand a mentee of your own age.

ul: Put the mentee's development first and be fair.
Never use information from mentoring to the mentee's harm.
Do not accept gifts or favours that would make you unable to be fair.
Stay within your competence; know when to refer.

blocks.p: Keep **brief notes** of goals, agreed actions and progress, stored securely. Do not keep a word-for-word record of everything said, notes on the mentee's private life, or nothing at all.

Review progress at agreed points: Are the goals being met? Is the relationship working? Do the meetings need to change? At the end, hold a **closing meeting** to review learning, celebrate progress and agree next steps, which may include informal contact or a new mentor. If the relationship is not working, talk honestly and agree a **no-fault end** and, if possible, a new match. Do not carry on for the sake of finishing the year, report the mentee for being difficult or let the relationship lapse in silence.

blocks.note: A good mentor works towards being no longer needed.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Running and evaluating a mentoring scheme

flow: Agree the **purpose** and how success will be measured (for example, retention after one year, goal completion, feedback)
Name a **scheme coordinator** and a steering group; get senior support
Decide **who takes part** (for example, all newly appointed officers) and how mentors are recruited
**Train mentors** before the scheme starts: the role and its limits, listening, questioning, feedback, goal-setting, confidentiality and boundaries
**Match** mentors and mentees on needs and goals, with both people's views
Run a **launch** where both meet, sign agreements and understand the support available
**Support and monitor** with check-ins, a progress review form and a route for problems
**Evaluate** at the end and improve the next round

blocks.p: Mentors should receive training **before** the scheme starts, so they understand the role, its limits and key skills. They do not supervise the mentees' daily work. A mentor should not be given too many mentees at once; one or two is usual. Mentors also need support and a place to share concerns, such as meetings with the coordinator and other mentors.

If the agency has offices in three parishes, plan for travel and technology: use video calls and messages for part of the contact, agree a regular schedule, keep calls private and secure, and arrange at least some face-to-face meetings. Make sure that mentees without good internet are not left out.

head: Measure
What it tells you
Example
rows: Retention rate = staff still employed / staff mentored x 100
Whether mentoring helps keep people
18 of 20 stay: 90%
Goal completion rate
Whether mentees achieve what they set out to
22 of 25 met all goals: 88%
Feedback from mentors and mentees
Quality of the relationship and what to improve
Short survey and discussion
Comparison with before or with a group without mentors
Whether the change is likely to be due to mentoring
14 of 20 stayed in the year before, against 18 of 20 now
Time invested
Cost of the scheme in hours
12 hours of meetings per mentee

ul: **Retention rate:** 24 new teachers were mentored and 21 were still in post after 18 months. 21 / 24 x 100 = 87.5%.
**Comparison:** in the previous year 20 of 25 stayed, which is 80%. The difference is 87.5 - 80 = 7.5 percentage points.

**Meeting time:** weekly 30-minute meetings for 10 weeks is 10 x 0.5 = 5 hours. Monthly 1.5-hour meetings for 12 months is 18 hours. Fortnightly 1-hour meetings for 6 months is about 13 meetings, so 13 hours.

blocks.p: The best evidence that a scheme is working combines **goal progress, feedback from both sides and retention compared with before**. The number of meetings booked, the cost of the launch or the length of the mentors' service does not show this. Be careful with conclusions: other things (pay, the job market, a new manager) also affect retention.

blocks.note: Do not publish names or comments from mentees in the evaluation. Report results as totals and themes, with their agreement.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: define mentoring and explain how it differs from coaching, line management, training and counselling.
name the main types: formal and informal, one-to-one, group, peer, reverse and e-mentoring.
describe the benefits to the mentee, mentor and organisation.
list the qualities of a good mentor and match mentors and mentees well.

terms: Mentor
The experienced person who guides another's growth.
Mentee
The person who receives guidance in a mentoring relationship.
Rapport
Mutual trust and understanding that lets mentor and mentee talk openly.
Mentoring agreement
The written understanding of goals, meetings, confidentiality and ending.
GROW
Goal, Reality, Options, Way forward: a model for a mentoring conversation.
SMART goal
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.
Active listening
Giving full attention and checking understanding, for example by summarising.
Open question
A question that cannot be answered with just yes or no.
Reflection
Thinking back over an experience to learn from it and plan the next step.
Boundaries
The limits a mentor keeps, such as not acting as manager or counsellor.
Reverse mentoring
A junior person guides a senior one, for example on digital tools.
Peer mentoring
Mentoring between colleagues at about the same level.
E-mentoring
Mentoring carried out mainly by email, messages and video calls.
Retention rate
Staff still employed after a period divided by staff at the start, as a percentage.
Dependency
When the mentee relies on the mentor for even small decisions.

c1.title: First meeting at a bank branch
c1.text: Orville Brown, an operations manager at a bank in Half-Way Tree, has agreed to mentor Kerry-Ann Powell, a new branch operations officer from another department. This is their first meeting. Kerry-Ann says she is nervous about the job and tells him her goal is 'to be more confident'. Orville has been in banking for twenty years and has many stories.

c2.title: A mentee who leans too hard
c2.text: In a Mandeville agency, Dr Camille Francis mentors Ricardo Ellis, a new officer. Over four months, Ricardo has started to message her late at night before every small decision. He recently asked her to lend him J$30,000 until payday and to speak to his manager about a transfer. His manager has asked Camille to 'tell me honestly what Ricardo's weak points are'.

c3.title: A ministry's mixed mentoring arrangements
c3.text: A ministry's headquarters in Kingston has regional offices in Montego Bay and Savanna-la-Mar. The HR director has set up three mentoring arrangements: young officers helping directors with new software; new officers in different offices supporting each other; and weekly video calls between a Kingston manager and an officer in Savanna-la-Mar. One long-running pair has met their goals.

c4.title: A scheme for new officers at a municipal corporation
c4.text: A municipal corporation in the west of Jamaica plans a mentoring scheme for newly appointed officers. The coordinator, Mr Delroy Smith, has 20 mentors who have volunteered and 28 new officers. Some mentors are senior and busy; one mentor has said she would take six mentees.

c5.title: Mentoring newly qualified teachers
c5.text: A group of schools in St Andrew mentored 24 newly qualified teachers for a school year. After 18 months, 21 were still teaching in the same schools, compared with 20 of 25 in the previous cohort, who had no mentors. 18 of the 24 mentees met all their goals.

questions.q: Orville wants to begin by learning about Kerry-Ann and how she feels about her new role. Which opening question is best?
o: Did you read the branch procedures manual before you came?
Don't you think you will find the work easy after your last job?
What are you hoping to get from your first months here?
Are you worried about meeting the targets for the quarter?
questions.why: An open question invites her to talk in her own words and shows interest in her goals. The other questions are closed or leading, and can make her defensive.

questions.q: Kerry-Ann says her goal is 'to be more confident'. What should Orville do?
o: Help her make it SMART, for example by presenting at three meetings
Accept the goal as stated, because confidence is personal and cannot really be measured
Replace it with a goal about learning the bank's systems, which he knows very well himself
Tell her to come back at the next meeting when she has a goal that is easier to measure
questions.why: A vague goal cannot be acted on or reviewed. The mentor's job is to help the mentee shape her own goal into a SMART one, not to accept it unchanged or to replace it with his own.

questions.q: Orville starts to describe at length how he handled his own first year at the bank. What is the best use of his experience?
o: Tell her story after story so that she can copy exactly what worked for him
Offer a short story once Kerry-Ann has explored her own ideas
Share his career history in full so that she knows he can be trusted
Avoid mentioning his own experience at all, so that he does not influence her
questions.why: Experience is most useful when it opens options, not when it tells the mentee what to do. A short story offered at the right time supports her thinking.

questions.q: Before they part, Orville and Kerry-Ann should agree the limits of confidentiality. Why?
o: So that Orville can pass the content of their meetings to her manager
So that she can be warned that anything she says may be used in her appraisal
So that the agreement can be ended whenever Orville wishes, without notice
So she knows what stays private and when something might have to be shared
questions.why: Mentees speak openly only if they know what stays private. Limits (for example, a serious risk of harm) are set out in advance, not discovered later.

questions.q: Ricardo asks Camille to lend him J$30,000 until payday. What should she do?
o: Lend the money, as it will help him to focus on his work again
Decline politely; a loan is outside the mentor's role
Lend it, but keep it quiet from the agency so that it is not seen as favour
Suggest he asks her manager friend instead, and offer to make the introduction
questions.why: A loan creates a financial tie and blurs the professional boundary. A mentor can help with budgeting skills or point to proper sources of help, but does not lend money.

questions.q: Ricardo wants Camille to speak to his manager to secure his transfer. What is the best response?
o: Agree, because helping the mentee's career is the main job of any mentor
Speak to the manager privately, but say that it is only her opinion
Explain she cannot influence it, and help him prepare
Tell him not to apply for a transfer at all this year
questions.why: A mentor does not fix outcomes for the mentee. She helps him think through his case, prepare and speak for himself, which builds his own ability.

questions.q: Ricardo messages her late at night before every small decision. What is the best step?
o: Ask him what he would do, and agree which decisions are his alone
Answer each message at once so that he never feels let down by her
Stop replying to his messages without telling him why she has stopped
Tell his manager that Ricardo cannot decide anything on his own yet
questions.why: Dependency defeats the purpose of mentoring. The mentor builds judgement by asking him to think first and by agreeing limits on contact, while staying supportive.

questions.q: Ricardo's manager asks Camille to 'tell me honestly what Ricardo's weak points are'. What should Camille say?
o: A short summary of what Ricardo has told her in the meetings about his struggles
Nothing at all, and she should avoid the manager from now on in future
A list of his mistakes, so that his manager can arrange extra training for him
That the meetings are confidential, so the manager should speak to Ricardo
questions.why: Reporting on the mentee would destroy trust and goes beyond the agreement. Politely stating confidentiality, and pointing to the proper line manager route, keeps the boundary.

questions.q: Young officers helping directors with software is an example of which type of mentoring, and what is its main benefit?
o: Group mentoring, because several people take part together at the same time
Reverse mentoring, because it passes skills upward and builds respect
Peer mentoring, because both parties work in the same ministry and building
Line management, because the director supervises the officers' daily work
questions.why: In reverse mentoring a junior person guides a senior one. It transfers current skills and helps the two groups understand each other.

questions.q: New officers in Montego Bay and Savanna-la-Mar supporting each other is best described as what?
o: Reverse mentoring, because they are newer than the managers and learn from them
A coaching scheme, because they practise a specific skill together
Peer mentoring, since they are at about the same level
E-mentoring, because they are in different parishes and meet at a distance
questions.why: Peer mentoring takes place between colleagues of similar level. E-mentoring depends on the channel, not the level; reverse mentoring means the junior guides the senior.

questions.q: The Kingston manager and the Savanna-la-Mar officer hold weekly 30-minute video calls for 10 weeks. How much meeting time is that, and what should they agree about the calls?
o: 10 hours, with a rule that calls are made only when the internet connection is good
3 hours, with notes of each call sent by email to the HR director
5 hours, with every call recorded and shared so the ministry has a full record
5 hours, with a set schedule and private, secure calls
questions.why: 10 x 0.5 hours = 5 hours. Remote mentoring needs a regular schedule, privacy and secure channels. Recording and sharing calls would break confidentiality.

questions.q: One pair has now met all their goals, and the mentee suggests that they should carry on meeting weekly 'forever'. What is the best step?
o: Hold a closing meeting and agree whether to keep informal contact
Continue the weekly meetings, as the mentee still values them a great deal
End the relationship without a meeting, so that she is not upset by it
Ask her manager to decide whether or not the mentoring continues
questions.why: A planned ending, with a review of what was learned and agreement about informal contact, lets the mentee move towards independence. Meetings that never end can create dependency.

questions.q: Which training topic is most important for the 20 mentors before the scheme starts?
o: How to supervise the daily work of the new officers they are matched with
How to write the yearly appraisal reports for the new officers they are matched with
The role and its limits, listening and confidentiality
How to decide which of the new officers deserve promotion first and fastest
questions.why: Mentors need to understand the role, its limits and key skills. Supervising, appraising and promoting are line management tasks, not mentoring.

questions.q: How should Mr Smith match 28 new officers with the 20 mentors?
o: By giving each mentor the officers who work closest to her own office
By the officers' goals, mentors' skills and both sides' views
By letting each of the senior mentors pick the officers she prefers
By drawing names from a hat, so that no one can complain about it
questions.why: Matching should be on needs, skills and the views of both people. Proximity, preference of seniors or chance ignores what makes the relationship work.

questions.q: One mentor says she will take six mentees. What should Mr Smith do?
o: Limit her to one or two, so each gets enough time
Accept, since 28 officers need mentors and she is willing to help
Accept, but reduce each of her meetings to ten minutes a month
Refuse her offer and remove her from the scheme as a mentor
questions.why: Quality of mentoring depends on time and attention. A small number of mentees per mentor is usual. A willing volunteer should be guided, not rejected or overloaded.

questions.q: After three months, what should the coordinator do to support the scheme?
o: Wait until the end of the year and then review the whole scheme at once
Ask each mentor to report the weaknesses that she sees in her mentee
Make the meetings compulsory and check the number of meetings held
Check in with pairs, gather feedback and deal with problems
questions.why: A scheme needs monitoring and support during the year. Reporting mentees' weaknesses breaks confidentiality, and counting meetings says nothing about quality.

questions.q: What was the retention rate for the mentored teachers?
How does retention compare with the previous cohort, and by how much?
o: 87.5% against 80%, a difference of 7.5 percentage points
87.5% against 80%, a difference of 7.5%
87.5% against 20%, a difference of 67.5 percentage points
87.5% against 75%, a difference of 12.5 percentage points
questions.why: The previous cohort retained 20 / 25 = 80%. 87.5 - 80 = 7.5 percentage points. The 7.5 is a difference between percentages, so it is in points.

questions.q: The principal says, 'The mentoring clearly caused the higher retention.' What is the best reply?
o: Correct, since the mentored group had a clearly higher figure
It is encouraging, but other factors may matter, so look at other evidence
Incorrect, because retention can never show the real value of mentoring
Correct, because 18 of the 24 mentees met all of their goals
questions.why: A higher retention rate is a good sign, but pay, the job market or new managers may also have changed. Combine retention with goal progress and feedback.

questions.q: Which additional evidence would best help judge whether the scheme is working?
o: The number of meetings entered in diaries and the cost of the launch event
The years of service that each mentor has completed in the school system
The number of mentors who attended the one-day training session
Goal progress, feedback from both sides and the earlier cohort
questions.why: Meaningful evidence shows results: goals achieved, views of those involved, and comparison with before. Diary entries, years of service and attendance measure activity, not results.
